zh: 先只考虑“不同字符串”的计数：如果没有去重要求，这就是普通的按位置 DP。难点在于同一个字符序列可能由很多组下标得到，必须只算一次；空子序列也算，前提是 x = y 且在 0..n 内。
设 f[p] 为“当前前缀能产生的、从 x 出发全程不越出 0..n、终点为 p 的不同字符串数”（含空串）。处理字符 c 时，把所有旧字符串末尾接上 c 得到 added（按 ±1 平移，越界的丢掉）；其中与旧集合重复的部分，恰好就是上一次处理同一字母 c 时追加出来的那批，所以记下 last[c] 并减去它。

若 x > n 或 y > n 直接输出 0。否则 f[x] = 1，对每个字符：r 时 added[j] = f[j−1]，l 时 added[j] = f[j+1]（越界位置为 0）；更新 f[j] = (f[j] + added[j] − last[c][j]) mod 10^9+7（注意取非负余数），再令 last[c] = added。最后输出 f[y]。复杂度 O(|s|·(n+1))。
en: Think first about counting distinct strings: without deduplication this would be an ordinary DP over positions. The difficulty is that the same character sequence can come from many index choices and must be counted once; the empty subsequence also counts, provided x = y and both lie in 0..n.

Let f[p] be the number of distinct strings from the current prefix (empty string included) that start at x, never leave 0..n, and end at p. When processing a character c, appending c to every old string gives added (shift by +/-1, dropping anything out of range). The part of added that duplicates old strings is exactly what was appended the last time the same letter c was processed, so remember it as last[c] and subtract it.

If x > n or y > n, print 0. Otherwise set f[x] = 1, and for each character: for r, added[j] = f[j-1]; for l, added[j] = f[j+1] (0 when out of range). Update f[j] = (f[j] + added[j] - last[c][j]) mod 10^9+7, keeping it non-negative, then set last[c] = added. Print f[y]. The cost is O(|s| * (n+1)).

explanationEn:
## Fixed source, the bounded number line, and the empty subsequence

fastprep/Flexport/flexport-distinct-moves.md at the fixed commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc states explicitly: the positions on the number line are 0..n, where n is the upper bound of the line; l changes j to j-1 and r changes j to j+1; return the number of distinct subsequences modulo 1000000007. This site counts distinct character sequences, so the same string coming from different indices is counted only once; this interpretation is supported by the detailed notes of the same problem in the Meesho version, and it is not claimed that the Flexport text itself contains those notes word for word. Flexport itself gives the complete ranges 1<=|s|<=1000 and 0<=x,y,n<=2500, which must not be silently narrowed to x,y<=n.

This site spells out what the bounded number line means: the starting position, the position after every step, and the end position must all lie in 0..n; a string that walks out of the domain is not a path on this line. There is no reflecting, staying put, or leaving and coming back, because those rules would change the j+-1 transitions that the original states explicitly. If x>n or y>n within the wide parameter ranges the original allows, the set of valid paths is empty and the answer is 0; this is an explicit interpretation of the original domain and does not pretend that the original additionally guarantees x,y<=n.

The Flexport original asks for distinct subsequences and does not require them to be non-empty. The fixed Meesho original of the same problem further states explicitly that deduplication is by character sequence and that zero or more elements may be deleted; this is supporting evidence across sources and does not pretend that Flexport wrote these detailed notes itself. Therefore the empty subsequence obtained by deleting every character counts: when x=y and it lies inside the domain, it contributes 1. With n=0 there is only position 0, and any non-empty move leaves the domain, so x=y=0 gives 1 and anything else gives 0. s itself must still be non-empty; the lower bound of the input length cannot be changed to 0.

The Flexport original example s=rrlrr, n=6, x=1, y=4 gives the answer 3; this site corrects it to 2 and keeps the original input. Enumerating all 32 index masks, there are only two valid character sequences, rrr and rrlrr; counting by indices would give 5, which is not 3 either. The original image points to the author's local machine at /Users/Eric/.../distinctMoves.png, cannot be read, and is not used as a basis for the correction. The other two public examples are derived by this site: rr from 0 to 1 counts r only once; rl on 0..1 from 0 back to 0 has two strings, the empty string and rl. The three-language code in the MDX only chooses/skips by index, so rr from 0 to 1 would wrongly give 2; no upstream code was executed.

## Approach

f[p] counts the distinct strings that the processed prefix can produce which start at x, always stay inside the domain, and end at p, including the empty string. The current character c moves by +-1; shifting the old f gives added[p], and out-of-domain contributions are not added. The new answer should be the old set united with all strings obtained by appending c, but the strings that the previous processing of the same character could already generate are added again. Maintain last[c][p], the contribution recorded the last time c was appended, update f[p]=f[p]+added[p]-last[c][p], and then set last[c]=added; take the non-negative modulus at every step.

## Proof of correctness

Initially there is only the empty string, which starts at the valid x and ends at x, so f[x]=1 is correct; with an out-of-domain start or end no path can exist, so 0 directly is correct. Assume the old f describes exactly the set of distinct valid strings. Appending the current character is injective: different prefix strings remain different after appending the same letter; the same string has a unique trajectory and end point, so shifting the counts by the displacement and excluding out-of-domain positions gives exactly the full set of newly appended strings.

If c has never appeared before, the appended set is disjoint from the old set. Otherwise, every string in the old set that ends with c can finish its embedding at the previous occurrence of c: the last c of its earlier embedding is no later than that position, and moving it there changes neither the character sequence nor the path. Therefore the intersection of the old set and the newly appended set is exactly the whole appended set recorded the last time c was processed. The set for the old prefix only grows, so nothing in the intersection is missed, and last[c] records the overlap correctly by end point. Subtracting this intersection once gives the union with nothing repeated and nothing missed. By induction, the final f[y] is the answer.

## Complexity and full bounds

Each character processes n+1 positions, for O(|s|(n+1)) time and O(n+1) space; the full 1000x2501 runs directly. The counts can grow exponentially, so all states and subtractions are normalized modulo 1000000007. Languages with negative remainders need an extra addition of the modulus. An out-of-range start or end cannot be used directly as an array index.

## Independent validation

The small-domain brute force enumerates all selection masks, puts the resulting character sequences into a set for deduplication, and simulates each path step by step while checking the domain. It exhaustively covers all lr strings of length 1..7, n=0..3, and x/y=0..4, including out-of-domain endpoints, 25400 cases in total.

The 163 oracle inputs use an independent canonical-next DAG: from the remaining input, choose either the earliest l or the earliest r as the next character, with the recursive meaning of continuing the count on the corresponding suffix; the same character sequence uses only its unique earliest embedding. Every state can also terminate when the current position equals y, contributing 1 for the empty suffix. The implementation goes from right to left and keeps the successor rows of the two next-character branches, without the reference's subtraction of the previous contribution. Short inputs are cross-checked against the mask-deduplication brute force, large data all use this independent DAG, and an unreduced big-integer DAG additionally checks the modular results.

The formal data cover full |s|=1000 with n=2500, x/y=2500, out-of-domain starts and ends, n=0, the empty-string contribution, boundaries that cannot be crossed, deduplication of repeated characters, repeated alternation, several modular wraparounds, and random cases. The two negative controls fail to subtract the repeated contribution and wrongly exclude the empty string, respectively; each counts as a kill only after exiting normally on all formal inputs.
